summary: This dissertation develops hardware-agnostic optimizations of fault-tolerant quantum computing by redesigning key building blocks including stabilizer measurement, state preparation, error correction, and logical gates to reduce qubit and time overhead. Techniques include flag-based fault tolerance with logarithmic ancilla requirements, deterministic state preparation for CSS codes with 100% yield, distance-four codes encoding six logical qubits using one-tenth the qubits of distance-five surface codes, and temporal encoding of lattice surgery reducing gate time by factors of 2–6.
motivation: Current quantum devices require hundreds to thousands of physical qubits per logical qubit due to error correction overhead, making the timeline for error-free quantum computing prohibitively long. Reducing both space and time costs of fault-tolerant components is essential to make large-scale quantum computation practical.
method: The work develops combinatorial proofs with flag fault tolerance for stabilizer measurement, uses flag circuits and measurement-based stabilizer state preparation to achieve deterministic encoding of ancilla states, optimizes planar error-correcting codes through postselection to improve code rates, and applies classical error-correcting codes to protect lattice surgery measurement results in the time domain, enabling faster computation without additional qubits.
result: Distance-three stabilizer measurement requires only $\lceil \log_2 w \rceil + 1$ ancilla qubits versus $O(w)$ previously; distance-four codes achieve comparable logical error rates to distance-five surface codes using 90% fewer qubits; temporal encoding of lattice surgery cuts computation time by factors of 2–6 depending on noise regime and target fidelity; deterministic Steane code state preparation uses 21 CNOT gates and Golay code preparation achieves 100% yield.
